title: Spiral Matrix II
description: Brute force to optimized: a visited-grid simulation versus tracking four shrinking boundaries directly.

Problem Summary: Given n, build an n by n grid, filled with the numbers 1 through n squared, placed in spiral order.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a number n, build an n by n grid, filled with the numbers 1 through n squared, placed in spiral order: starting at the top left, moving right across the top, down the right side, left across the bottom, up the left side, and continuing inward.

blocks.title: Analogy: Coiling a Rope Inward
blocks.text: Picture laying a rope down flat starting at the top left corner of a square room, walking right along the top wall, then turning to walk down the right wall, then left along the bottom wall, then up the left wall, and continuing to coil inward every time a wall is reached. Numbering each footstep along the way, in order, produces exactly the spiral pattern this problem asks for.

blocks.caption: The spiral path: right, down, left, up, repeating inward

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 3
Starting at 1 in the top left, the path moves right to 3, down to 5, left to 7, and spirals inward to finish at 9 in the center.
Example: n = 1
A grid with a single cell has nowhere to spiral, so the answer is simply [[1]].
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what shape the spiral movement rule actually traces out.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The spiral movement rule, keep going until blocked, then turn, sounds like it needs careful step by step tracking of every visited cell.

Observation 2: But the actual shape traced out by that rule is completely predictable: it is always a rectangle that shrinks inward by exactly one layer every time all four of its sides have been filled.

Observation 3: If the shape is fully predictable, the four edges of that shrinking rectangle, top, bottom, left, and right, are all the information needed to know exactly which cells to fill next, no per-cell visited check required.

Observation 4: Filling each edge completely in one pass, then shrinking the corresponding boundary inward by one, reproduces the exact same spiral order without ever asking "have I been here before".
That reasoning alone already replaces the entire visited-grid idea with just four numbers.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most literal approach is to walk one cell at a time, keeping track of a current direction (right, down, left, or up) and a separate grid recording which cells have already been visited. Whenever the next cell in the current direction would go out of bounds or has already been visited, turn clockwise to the next direction.
Step by step algorithm

items: Start at the top left cell, moving right, and fill it with 1.
Before each step, check whether continuing in the current direction would go out of bounds or land on an already visited cell.
If so, turn clockwise to the next direction.
Move one cell in the current direction, fill it with the next number, and mark it visited.
Repeat until every cell from 1 to n squared has been placed.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: move one cell at a time, turning when blocked or out of bounds

codes.python:
def generate_matrix(n):
    matrix = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]     # the answer grid, starts empty
    visited = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]  # separate grid tracking where we've already been
    directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]  # right, down, left, up
    row, col, dir_index = 0, 0, 0
    for num in range(1, n * n + 1):
        matrix[row][col] = num                # fill the current cell with the next number
        visited[row][col] = True               # mark this cell as visited
        dr, dc = directions[dir_index]
        next_row, next_col = row + dr, col + dc
        # turn clockwise if the next cell is out of bounds or already visited
        if not (0 <= next_row < n and 0 <= next_col < n) or visited[next_row][next_col]:
            dir_index = (dir_index + 1) % 4
            dr, dc = directions[dir_index]
        row, col = row + dr, col + dc
    return matrix


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 3
    for row in generate_matrix(n):
        print(row)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A separate visited grid, distinct from the answer matrix itself, exists specifically because the answer matrix stores the spiral numbers, while visited only needs to track true or false for whether a cell has been filled yet.

The direction check happens before moving, looking one step ahead to decide whether to turn, rather than moving first and checking afterward, since moving into an invalid cell and then correcting would require undoing that move.

directions is stored as an ordered list of exactly four row-and-column offsets, cycled through with modulo 4, which is what makes "turn clockwise" a simple index increment rather than a chain of if/else branches.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because checking "in bounds and not yet visited" before every step correctly reproduces the spiral shape, turning at exactly the right moments.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every cell is filled exactly once.
Space: O(n squared) extra, for the separate visited grid, on top of the answer grid itself.

Limitation: the separate visited grid is redundant bookkeeping. The exact shape of the spiral is fully predictable in advance: it always shrinks inward as a rectangle with four clean edges, so there is no real need to check "have I been here" one cell at a time.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why per-cell visited checking works but is unnecessary: the spiral's shape is not actually unpredictable, it is a rectangle shrinking inward one layer at a time, in a fixed, knowable pattern.

What the visited grid costs: an entire extra n by n grid of bookkeeping, just to answer a question, "have I been here", that the shrinking rectangle shape already answers for free.

Can the shape be tracked without per-cell checks: yes, four simple boundary values, top, bottom, left, and right, describe exactly which region is left to fill at every point.

How does filling work with just those four values: fill one full edge completely, in the correct spiral direction, then shrink that specific boundary inward by one before moving to the next edge.

The core idea: track four shrinking boundaries directly, fill each edge completely, no visited grid needed at all.

Instead of checking visited status cell by cell, track the four edges of the region still left to fill: a top row, a bottom row, a left column, and a right column. Fill each edge completely in one pass, then shrink that boundary inward before moving to the next edge.
This removes the need for any separate visited tracking at all, the four boundaries alone are enough to know exactly where to fill next.
9. Optimized Solution

Fill the top row left to right, then shrink the top boundary down by one. Fill the right column top to bottom, then shrink the right boundary in by one. If a row still remains, fill the bottom row right to left and shrink the bottom boundary up by one. If a column still remains, fill the left column bottom to top and shrink the left boundary in by one. Repeat until the boundaries cross.
Dry run for n = 3

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: fill each shrinking edge completely, no visited tracking needed

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the spiral pattern really is a nested sequence of shrinking rectangular rings, and each ring's top row, right column, bottom row, and left column can be filled completely and independently, in that exact order, without ever needing to check whether a cell has already been visited, since the four boundaries themselves guarantee no cell is ever touched twice. The two guard checks, confirming a row or column still remains before filling the bottom row or left column, exist specifically to handle the case where the shrinking rectangle has collapsed to a single row or column, where filling all four edges would otherwise double count that same row or column.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The four boundaries, top, bottom, left, and right, start at the matrix's own edges and shrink inward by exactly one after each of their corresponding edges is fully filled.

The bottom row and left column fills are wrapped in their own guard checks specifically because, once the shrinking rectangle collapses to a single row or a single column, filling all four edges unconditionally would refill cells that the top row or right column fill already handled.

num is incremented once per cell filled, in the exact order cells are visited, which is what guarantees the numbers 1 through n squared land in true spiral order rather than needing a separate position-to-number calculation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same as the brute force, and unavoidable since every cell must be filled.
Space: O(1) extra, just four boundary values, a genuine reduction from the O(n squared) visited grid used before.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is recognizing that a seemingly complex movement rule, turning whenever blocked, actually follows a completely predictable shrinking rectangle, which means the entire process can be planned out with just four numbers instead of tracking every individual cell's visited status.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the guard checks, top less than or equal to bottom, left less than or equal to right, before filling the bottom row and left column, which can double-fill cells or go out of bounds for non-square remaining shapes like n = 1 or n = 2.
Mixing up which boundary shrinks after which edge is filled.
Off by one errors in the loop ranges for each of the four edges.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a great test of whether a candidate can replace "step by step simulation with bookkeeping" with "a cleaner structural model" of the same process. Explicitly naming the four boundaries and explaining why they remove the need for a visited grid shows strong spatial reasoning.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the visited grid", think: track four shrinking boundaries, top, bottom, left, right, instead.
If the interviewer says "why do you need the guard checks", think: without them, a collapsed single row or column gets filled twice.
If the interviewer says "can you do this with O(1) extra space", think: the four boundary approach already achieves that, beyond the required output itself.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why do the bottom row and left column fills specifically need their own guard checks, but the top row and right column do not?
Can you adapt this same four-boundary technique to traverse an existing matrix in spiral order, rather than building one?
How would the boundary tracking change for a rectangular, non-square matrix?
What is the relationship between the number of "rings" this spiral has and the value of n?
Can you fill the spiral starting from a different corner, or in a counterclockwise direction, using the same boundary idea?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Spiral Matrix, the reverse problem, reading an existing matrix in spiral order instead of building one, which reuses the exact same four-boundary technique.
Any 2D simulation problem where a step by step movement rule actually traces out a fully predictable geometric shape, worth checking before reaching for a visited grid.
Matrix rotation and layer based problems in general, which often process a matrix ring by ring, the same shrinking boundary idea applied to a different operation.
Boundary or two-pointer style tracking used to replace an auxiliary data structure whenever the region of interest shrinks in a predictable, well defined way.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches use O(n squared) time, unavoidable since every cell in the output must be filled. The brute force approach additionally uses O(n squared) extra space for its visited grid, while the boundary tracking approach uses only O(1) extra space, a genuine reduction in auxiliary memory.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a movement simulation that is actually a fully predictable shrinking rectangle, replacing per-cell visited tracking with four boundary variables.

Core Idea: track four boundaries, top, bottom, left, and right; fill each edge completely in the correct spiral direction, then shrink the corresponding boundary inward by one, repeating until the boundaries cross.
Time: O(n squared) for both versions, unavoidable since every cell must be filled.
Space: O(n squared) extra for the brute force's visited grid, O(1) extra for the boundary tracking version.
Most Important Observation: a movement rule that sounds like it needs per-cell bookkeeping can sometimes be replaced entirely by recognizing the fixed geometric shape it always traces out.

Interview Difficulty: easy to simulate step by step with a visited grid; recognizing and correctly implementing the four-boundary shrinking rectangle, including its guard checks, is what distinguishes a strong answer.
One line memory trick: four shrinking boundaries, fill each edge completely, guard the last row and column.
